common_name: Red Rustproof Oat (Heirloom Southern Winter Oat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in fall across the Deep South and Gulf Coast so plants establish a rosette before winter; this old landrace is only half-hardy and needs the mild winters of USDA zones 7-9 rather than true Northern cold.

directions: Red Rustproof arrived in the Deep South around 1849, reportedly carried home from the Mexican War, and by the early 1900s it was the dominant winter oat grown from Georgia through Texas because of its strong immunity to crown rust, a disease that regularly wiped out other oat stands. Drill or broadcast in fall into worked ground; the crop overwinters as a leafy rosette on cotton-worn soils and resumes vigorous growth once days lengthen in late winter. It is markedly less cold-hardy than northern oat types, so it belongs in mild-winter regions rather than areas with hard, prolonged freezes. Cut and thresh in early summer once the panicles dry to gold, saving the light, thin-hulled grain for livestock feed or replanting the following fall.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical bulletins

planting.note: Broadcast or drill at the earliest workable spring date on the Northern Plains and Corn Belt; Kherson is an early, drought-tolerant spring oat rather than a fall-sown type.

directions: Kherson was brought into the United States in 1896 from the Kherson region of southern Russia by way of the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station, and within twenty years it had become one of the most widely sown oats across the Great Plains and Corn Belt thanks to its short season and unusual drought tolerance. Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring; the crop germinates in cool soil and races to maturity ahead of the worst summer heat, which is what made it so valuable on dry, marginal prairie ground before irrigation was common. It tillers modestly and stands a bit shorter than many modern oats, so it tolerates lean soil without lodging heavily. Harvest when straw and hulls turn pale gold, then thresh promptly since the loose hull shatters somewhat more readily than modern oat varieties.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical bulletins
South Dakota State University Extension oat variety records

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Trebi was developed for irrigated Western valleys and also performs well as a rain-fed spring barley on the Northern Plains.

directions: Trebi was collected by USDA plant explorer Mark Carleton in Russia in the early 1900s and released after testing by the USDA Office of Cereal Investigations, quickly becoming a benchmark six-row spring barley across irrigated valleys of the Western United States for its high yield and strong straw. Sow into a firm, fertile seedbed in early spring; it responds especially well to irrigation but also holds up under rain-fed Northern Plains conditions. The stiff-strawed plant resists lodging better than many barleys of its era, letting it carry a heavy head of grain without falling over before harvest. Cut and thresh once the heads dry to straw-gold, and use the plump kernels for livestock feed, malting trials, or seed increase.
sources: USDA Office of Cereal Investigations historical records
University of California Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education Program
